source_text: Ostensa sit nunc anima per carnem, si constiterit illam ostendendam quoquo modo fuisse, id est incognitam sibi et nobis. Quamquam in hoc vana distinctio est; quasi nos seorsum ab anima simus, cum totum, quod sumus, anima sit. Denique sine anima nihil sumus, ne hominis quidem, sed cadaveris nomen. Si ergo ignoramus animam, ipsa se ignorat. Itaque superest hoc solummodo inspicere, an se anima hic ignorarit, ut nota quoquo modo fieret. Opinor, sensualis est animae natura. Adeo, nihil animale sine sensu; nihil sensuale sine anima. Et ut impressius dixerim, animae anima sensus est. Igitur cum omnibus anima sentire praestet, et ipsa sentiat omnium etiam sensus, nedum qualitates, qui verisimile est, ut ipsa sensum sui ab initio sortita non sit? Unde illi, scire quod interdum sibi sit necessarium, ex naturalium necessitate, si non scit suam qualitatem, cui quid necessarium est? Hoc quidem in omni anima recognoscere est; notitiam sui dico; sine qua notitia sui nulla anima se ministrare potuisset. Puto autem magis hominem, animal solum rationale, compotem et animam esse sortitum, quae illum facit animal rationale, ipsa in primis rationalis. Porro, quomodo rationalis, quae efficit hominem rationale animal, si ipsa rationem suam nescit, ignorans semetipsam? Sed adeo non ignorat, ut auctorem, et arbitrum, et statum suum norit. Nihil adhuc de Deo discens, Deum nominat: nihil adhuc de judicio ejus admittens, Deo commendare se dicit. Nihil magis audiens, quam spem nullam esse post mortem, et bene et male defuncto cuique imprecatur. Plenius haec prosequitur libellus quem scripsimus de Testimonio animae. Alioquin, si anima semetipsam ignorans erat ab initio, nihil a Christo cognovisse debuerat, nisi qualis esset. Nunc autem non effigiem suam discit a Christo, sed salutem. Propterea Filius Dei descendit, et animam subiit; non ut ipsa se anima cognosceret in Christo, sed ut Christum in semetipsa; non enim se ignorando de salute periclitatur, sed Dei Verbum. Vita, inquit, manifestata est; non anima, etc.: Veni, inquit, animam salvam facere: non dixit, ostendere. Ignorabamus nimirum animam, licet invisibilem, nasci et mori, nisi corporaliter exhiberetur. Ignoravimus plane resurrecturam cum carne. Hoc erit quod Christus manifestavit. Sed et hoc non aliter in se, quam in Lazaro aliquo, cujus caro non erat animalis, ita nec anima carnalis. Quid ergo amplius innotuit nobis de animae ignoratae retro dispositione? Quid invisibile ejus fuit, quod visibilitatem per carnem desideraret?
pass_a_gloss: Let the soul be shown now through the flesh, if it has been established that it was to be shown in some way, that is, unknown to itself and to us. Although in this matter there is a vain distinction; as if we were separate from the soul, when the whole thing that we are is soul. Finally, without the soul we are nothing, not even a human being, but the name of a corpse. If therefore we are ignorant of the soul, it itself is ignorant. And so it remains only to examine this, whether the soul has been ignorant of itself here, so that it might become known in some way. I think that the nature of the soul is sensual. So much so, that there is nothing animal without sense; nothing sensual without soul. And so that I may speak more emphatically, the sense is the soul of the soul. Therefore, since the soul provides the ability to perceive for all things, and it itself perceives all the senses, and even the qualities, which is likely, how is it that it did not have the sense of itself from the beginning? Whence it is necessary for it to know what is sometimes necessary for it, from the necessity of natural things, if it does not know its own quality, for which what is necessary? This indeed is to be recognized in every soul; I say the knowledge of itself; without which knowledge of itself no soul could have taken care of itself. I think, however, that man, the only rational animal, has been endowed with a soul, which makes him a rational animal, and this soul is rational above all. Furthermore, how is it rational, which makes man a rational animal, if it does not know its own reason, being ignorant of itself? But it does not ignore itself so much, that it knows its author, and judge, and state. Not yet learning about God, it names God; not yet admitting its judgment, it says it commends itself to God. Hearing nothing more than that there is no hope after death, and it curses each one who has died well and badly. This is more fully pursued in the booklet that we wrote about the Testimony of the Soul. Otherwise, if the soul was ignorant of itself from the beginning, it would not have known anything from Christ, except what kind it was. Now, however, it does not learn its own image from Christ, but salvation. Therefore, the Son of God descended, and subjected the soul; not so that the soul might know itself in Christ, but so that it might know Christ in itself; for it is not endangered by ignorance of itself regarding salvation, but by the Word of God. Life, he says, has been made manifest; not the soul, etc.; I came, he says, to save the soul; he did not say, to show. We were indeed ignorant of the soul, although invisible, being born and dying, unless it was exhibited bodily. We were completely ignorant of the resurrection with the flesh. This is what Christ has made manifest. But also this not otherwise in itself, than in some Lazarus, whose flesh was not animal, so also the soul was not carnal. What therefore has become more known to us about the previously unknown disposition of the soul? What was its invisible thing, which desired visibility through the flesh?
pass_b_english: Let the soul now be displayed through the flesh, if it has been established that it was supposed to be shown in some way — that is, unknown both to itself and to us. The distinction drawn here is empty; it acts as though we exist apart from the soul, when in fact the soul is the whole of what we are. In the end, without the soul we are nothing — not even human, just a corpse's name. So if we are ignorant of the soul, the soul itself is ignorant. The only thing left, then, is to examine whether the soul has been ignorant of itself here, so that it might become known in some way. I hold that the soul's nature is sensual; indeed, nothing animal exists without sense, and nothing sensual exists without soul. To put it more forcefully: sense is the soul of the soul. Since the soul supplies perception to everything, and itself perceives all the senses — even the qualities, which is likely — how could it not have possessed the sense of itself from the beginning? Otherwise, how would it know, from the necessity of natural things, what it sometimes needs, if it does not know its own quality, the very thing for which something is necessary? This self-knowledge is to be recognized in every soul; I mean the knowledge of itself, without which no soul could have taken care of itself. I think, however, that man — the only rational animal — has been endowed with a soul that makes him rational, and that soul is rational above all. How could it be rational, making man a rational animal, if it does not know its own reason, being ignorant of itself? Yet it does not ignore itself so completely; it knows its author, its judge, and its state. Without yet learning about God, it names God; without yet admitting its judgment, it says it commends itself to God. Hearing nothing more than that there is no hope after death, it curses each one who has died, both well and badly. This is pursued more fully in the booklet we wrote on the Testimony of the Soul. Otherwise, if the soul was ignorant of itself from the beginning, it would not have known anything from Christ except what sort of thing it was. Now, however, it does not learn its own image from Christ, but salvation. Therefore the Son of God descended and subjected the soul — not so that the soul might know itself in Christ, but that it might know Christ in itself; for it is not endangered by ignorance of itself regarding salvation, but by the Word of God. "Life has been made manifest," he says; "not the soul," etc. (1 John 1:2). "I came," he says, "to save the soul"; he did not say, "to show it." We were indeed ignorant of the soul — even though invisible — being born and dying, unless it was exhibited bodily. We were completely ignorant that it would rise again with the flesh. This is what Christ has made manifest. But even this manifestation occurs in the soul no differently than in some Lazarus, whose flesh was not animal, so neither was his soul carnal. What, then, has become more known to us about the soul's previously unknown disposition? What invisible thing of the soul desired visibility through the flesh?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains all nuances of agency and modality. The scripture citation (1 John 1:2) added in Pass B for 'Vita... manifestata est' is a correct identification of the allusion/quote. The title 'Knowledge of the Soul' correctly names the central thought of the passage.
